title: First-wave Second Life rivals and successors (2000s-2010s) and why they failed
summary: Across sixteen first-wave rivals and successors of Second Life, the pattern is consistent: products built as "a place to hang out in 3D" died, and the survivors are the ones with a concrete loop that gives users a reason to log in and spend on each other. There.com closed on 9 March 2010 with membership still growing because sponsor, developer and land-fee revenue shrank in the recession; it returned in May 2012 as a $10/month hobby club. Blue Mars bet on CryEngine 2 in 2009, burned over $13M, cut staff by two-thirds by January 2011, and donated its tech to a university in 2012 after chasing three audiences and two lighter clients. The Sims Online peaked at roughly 105,000 subscribers in 2003 behind a box-plus-subscription wall and was shut on 1 August 2008 after the EA-Land free-client rebrand failed to ship. PlayStation Home's 41M "members" were cumulative registrations; Sony called it a niche, stopped developer payouts, and closed it on 31 March 2015 rather than port to PS4. Google Lively (20 users per room, ~10k actives) and Cloud Party (acqui-hired by Yahoo, closed 21 Feb 2014) were ended by parent-company priorities. The VR wave repeated the hardware mistake: High Fidelity raised ~$73M, found daily VR users were ~100x below Rosedale's projection and peak rooms held ~90 people, and shut its world on 15 Jan 2020; Sansar's concurrency stayed "in the low hundreds" and Linden Lab sold it in March 2020; vTime XR closed abruptly in October 2025 over an unpatchable Unity flaw. Survivors (Active Worlds since 1995, Entropia's withdrawable PED economy, Habbo's teen goods, IMVU's 7M MAU avatar chat with 400k user products a month) share free entry, user-to-user economies, and low fixed costs; Habbo's 2012 moderation scandal, which cost it two investors and two-thirds of staff, shows safety is existential. Caveat: WebFetch could not resolve any host in this sandbox and the shared search budget ran out, so facts come from quoted search extracts of the cited pages and several figures are flagged unverified.
design_implications: Define the purpose loop (collaborative building with ownership, scarce events, a tradable economy) before the renderer, and measure success by peak concurrent users per region rather than registrations.

Target hardware the audience already owns: web/desktop/mobile-first with scalable fidelity; VR is an optional view, never a requirement, so high-end graphics must degrade gracefully to integrated GPUs and phones.
Make revenue user-to-user (creator goods, land rent flowing to creators, event tickets) so income scales with community activity, not with a handful of sponsors or ad budgets.
No subscription or box-price wall at entry; free-to-enter with premium tiers for creators and land, following IMVU/Habbo/Second Life rather than The Sims Online or There's 2012 relaunch.

Treat creator tooling (avatar customisation, animation library, in-world editing, import pipelines) as the core product; ship AI NPCs, bots and spectacle only after the basic self-expression loop is excellent.
Build trust and safety in from the first release (age-gating, verified-adult spaces, moderation tooling, transparent reporting) because one exposé can remove investors and advertisers within weeks.

Guarantee portability and continuity: exportable assets and inventories, open formats, and a pre-published escrowed sunset plan (server images, export tools, community handover) so the world is never hostage to a corporate pivot or an engine vulnerability.
Avoid single-vendor lock-in on engine, console store or headset ecosystem; keep engine and distribution as replaceable layers.
Keep fixed costs low enough to survive a recession on organic revenue while funding growth from creator-economy take rates.
Engineer for crowd concurrency (hundreds in one space, thousands per event) since large shared moments are what the surviving worlds monetise.
open_questions: There.com: total venture funding and peak concurrent users (the ~$37M figure and 2003-2005 subscriber counts were not confirmed before the search budget ran out).
PlayStation Home: Sony's actual revenue and active-user figures, and whether it was ever profitable as claimed around 2011; no primary source surfaced.
Sansar: Linden Lab's actual spend (the oft-quoted $75M is unverified) and Steam concurrent-user data.
Blue Mars: exact PC system requirements and the number of land parcels sold to third-party developers.
Kaneva: funding raised and the reason for the 14 November 2016 closure.
Cloud Party: funding, user counts and the price Yahoo paid.
Entropia: audited MindArk revenue (from its listed-company annual reports) versus self-reported transaction volumes.
Habbo: current MAU and whether Hotel Hideaway has materially replaced desktop revenue.

All facts should be re-verified by direct fetch of Wikipedia, Engadget, TechCrunch, VentureBeat and company blogs; this run could not fetch any page directly due to DNS resolution failures in the sandbox.

claims.claim: After a June 2012 Channel 4 investigation, Sulake muted all Habbo chat, Balderton sold its ~13% stake, revenue recovered to only ~75% by August, and headcount fell from about 90 to 30 by October 2012; 2011 revenue had been US$78.7M.

checks.note: TechCrunch unreachable (DNS). Chat mute and Balderton's 13% exit match the checker's recollection of the June 2012 coverage. The '75% recovery by August' and '~90 to 30 headcount' numbers come from a RageZone forum repost and a fan wiki, not primary sources; Sulake had several hundred staff in 2008-2010 and reported ~40% cuts in late 2012, so '90 to 30' may be garbled or one office. '$78.7M 2011 revenue' is a USD conversion of a EUR filing figure; quote the EUR original. Weakest-sourced claim in the brief.

Doubtful figures: Sulake reported revenue in euros (2011 on the order of EUR 55-60M), so 'US$78.7M' needs its conversion basis; 'about 90 to 30' headcount is far below Sulake's known 2011-12 staffing (well over 100) and may describe one office or function; '~75% recovery' is a company statement. checks.note: Wikipedia unreachable (DNS). Likely date error (background knowledge, not verified here): Jon 'NEVERDIE' Jacobs bought the $100,000 asteroid/Club NEVERDIE in October 2005; 2008 is the Guinness Gamer's Edition listing year. Treasure Island $26,500 (Dec 2004) is correct. 500,000 users on 17 Oct 2006 is a MindArk self-report relayed by Wikipedia. The $242M/$64M deposit/withdrawal figures come from a MindArk PRNewswire release the brief dates to 2025 but which appears to be Dec 2024; confirm whether cumulative since 2003 and note that deposits fund MindArk's services, so 'net-extractive' overstates player losses.

Date error: Jon 'NEVERDIE' Jacobs bought Club NEVERDIE for US$100,000 in October 2005, not 2008; 2008 is the Guinness Gamer's Edition that listed it. Treasure Island ($26,500, Dec 2004) and the 500,000-account milestone (Oct 2006) are correct. The $242M deposits / $64M withdrawals figures come from a MindArk press release whose PRNewswire id (302341829) dates it to December 2024, so 'as of 2025' should read 'as of late 2024'; numbers are self-reported and unchecked.

The brief omits the successors that actually reached scale: Roblox (tens of millions DAU, creator payouts near US$1B/yr) and VRChat (six-figure peak concurrency at New Year's events, desktop+VR, creator economy launched 2023, ~30% layoffs in 2024). A successor plan should benchmark against these, not only against 2000s-2010s failures. (Background knowledge, not verified in this run.)

Second Life itself is the control case the brief under-weights: still ~US$600M+/yr in user-to-user transactions, hundreds of thousands of monthly users, and a 2024-2025 mobile viewer. Its survival on user-paid land fees plus a Linden-dollar exchange shows land revenue is fragile only when it depends on brand sponsors rather than residents.

The 2021-2023 blockchain worlds (Decentraland, The Sandbox) repeated the purpose-vacuum pattern: DAU in the low thousands despite billion-dollar token valuations. The brief's 'concurrency not registrations' rule generalises to 'active users, not token holders'.

Meta's Horizon Worlds repeated the premature-hardware bet at vastly larger budget (Reality Labs cumulative losses above US$60B, 2020-2024) and then ported to mobile/web, reinforcing the 'ship for hardware the audience owns' implication.

Likely factual correction for the brief: Club NEVERDIE/asteroid was purchased for $100,000 in October 2005, not 2008 (2008 is the Guinness listing year). Weakest-sourced numbers overall are Habbo's '90 to 30 headcount' and '75% revenue recovery' (forum repost + fan wiki) and Sansar's 'low hundreds' concurrency (an observer's estimate, should be attributed to Wagner James Au).

Verification limitation: no cited URL could be fetched (WebFetch DNS failures on every host, WebSearch budget already exhausted at 200/200, curl denied), so whether each source actually says what is attributed to it is unverified for all ten claims; verdicts rest on checker knowledge and a follow-up run with network access should re-fetch the ten URLs.

The successors that actually worked after this wave were Roblox (tens of millions of daily users, creator payouts in the high hundreds of millions of dollars per year) and VRChat (user-built worlds via a Unity SDK, VR optional, roughly half of users on flat screens); they, not Sansar or High Fidelity, should be the design benchmark for the purpose loop, optional VR and creator economy.

High Fidelity's open-source codebase was forked by its community (Vircadia, later Overte) after the company withdrew its apps, and Wookey kept Sansar alive: open source and transferable server software are the proven 'sunset insurance' the brief recommends.

IMVU's VCOIN (Nov 2020) was the first transferable token to receive an SEC no-action letter; any successor with a withdrawable currency inherits that regulatory template, and Entropia's fixed 10:1 PED shows such economies run net-extractive from players.

Meta's Horizon Worlds absorbed multi-billion-dollar annual Reality Labs losses and still pivoted to mobile in 2024-25, the most recent confirmation of the 'wrong hardware bet' pattern; it belongs in the pattern list.

Habbo's 2024 relaunch of a 2005-era client (Habbo Hotel: Origins) revived engagement, evidence that preserved community identity and nostalgia are reusable assets (same lesson as There.com's 2025 return surge and the PS Home fan revival).

The incumbent the successor must beat, Second Life itself, is absent from the brief: it still runs with hundreds of thousands of monthly users, a user-to-user economy in the hundreds of millions of dollars per year, and shipped an official mobile viewer in 2024.
